section-85: Plato (427-347 BCE), a disciple of Socrates and founder of the Academy in Athens, wrote 'The Republic' (subtitled 'Concerning Justice'), 'The Statesman' and 'The Laws'. In the Republic, he rejected popular views of justice: Cephalus (speaking the truth and paying debts), Polemarchus (doing good to friends and harm to enemies), Thrasymachus ('justice is the interest of the stronger') and Glaucon (justice as a convention born of fear).

Plato's own theory: justice is 'doing one's own work and not meddling with what is not one's own'. Corresponding to the three parts of the human soul - reason, spirit and appetite - there are three classes in the state: rulers (philosophers, with the virtue of wisdom), auxiliaries or warriors (courage) and producers (temperance). Justice is the harmony that results when each class performs its function under the guidance of reason. It is both individual (harmony of the soul) and social. Critics (Karl Popper, 'The Open Society and Its Enemies', 1945) called it totalitarian, as it subordinates the individual to the state and creates rigid classes.
section-86: Plato considered education 'the one great thing'; Rousseau called the Republic 'the finest treatise on education ever written'. Education was a state responsibility, compulsory for both men and women, aimed at developing character and selecting rulers. The first stage (up to about 20 years) included music (literature, poetry, arts - censored to promote virtue) for the soul and gymnastics for the body.

Those who showed ability went on to higher education (20-30 years) in mathematics, geometry, astronomy and the sciences; the best studied dialectics (philosophy) from 30 to 35; then gained practical experience in administration for 15 years; and at 50, the philosopher-kings would rule, having attained knowledge of the 'Form of the Good'. Plato's theory emphasised equal education for women, merit and lifelong learning, but has been criticised for censorship and an elitist system.
section-87: Plato's communism applied only to the ruling classes (guardians and auxiliaries), not to the producers. It had two parts: (1) communism of property - guardians would have no private property, live in common barracks, eat together and receive necessities from the producers, so they would not be corrupted by greed; and (2) communism of wives and children (abolition of the family) - marriages would be arranged by the state through festivals for eugenic purposes, children would be brought up in state nurseries without knowing their parents, so that guardians would regard all as one family and be free from selfish attachments.

Its purpose was political - to ensure that rulers devoted themselves fully to the public good and to unify the state - not economic equality. It differs from Marxian communism, which is economic, applies to all society and aims at abolition of classes. Aristotle criticised it: 'what is common to the greatest number has the least care bestowed upon it'; abolishing the family would weaken affection; and it ignores human nature.
section-88: Plato's ideal state is described in the Republic. Its features: (1) rule by philosopher-kings - 'until philosophers are kings, or the kings and princes of this world have the spirit and power of philosophy... cities will never have rest from their evils'; (2) division of society into three functional classes based on aptitude (the 'myth of metals' - rulers of gold, auxiliaries of silver, producers of iron and bronze, with mobility based on merit); (3) justice as harmony; (4) state-controlled education; (5) communism of property and family for guardians; (6) equality of women, who could become guardians; and (7) the rule of reason rather than law.

Plato called it a 'pattern laid up in heaven'. In 'The Laws', written later, he proposed a 'second-best' state ruled by law, with private property and family. Criticisms: it is utopian, authoritarian, ignores individual freedom and consent, has no checks on rulers and treats producers as passive. Nevertheless, Plato raised fundamental questions about justice, education and the qualifications of rulers.
section-89: Aristotle (384-322 BCE), Plato's student and tutor of Alexander the Great, founded the Lyceum. In 'Politics', he classified constitutions based on two criteria: (1) the number of rulers (one, few or many) and (2) the purpose of rule (the common good - 'true' or 'normal' forms; or the interest of the rulers - 'perverted' forms). True forms: monarchy (rule of one for all), aristocracy (rule of the virtuous few) and polity (rule of the many in the common interest). Perverted forms: tyranny (one for himself), oligarchy (the rich few for themselves) and democracy (the poor many for themselves).

He believed constitutions change in a cycle: monarchy degenerates into tyranny, which is replaced by aristocracy, which degenerates into oligarchy, followed by polity, which degenerates into democracy, and then back to monarchy. Aristotle based his classification on a study of 158 Greek constitutions, which shows his empirical method. Criticisms: the classification is based on Greek city-states, does not fit modern nation-states, and his use of 'democracy' as a perverted form differs from modern usage.
section-90: Aristotle distinguished the ideal state (best in theory) from the best practicable state (best for most states under normal conditions). The best practicable state is the 'polity', a mixed constitution combining elements of oligarchy (rule of the rich) and democracy (rule of the poor), based on the principle of the 'golden mean' (moderation, avoiding extremes). It is dominated by a large middle class, which is neither too rich (arrogant) nor too poor (envious), and therefore stable and fair.

Features include rule of law (law as 'reason unaffected by desire'), moderate property qualifications for citizenship, participation of citizens in deliberation and justice, and a balance of interests. Aristotle's ideal of the middle class and mixed constitution influenced later ideas of constitutional government, checks and balances (Polybius, Cicero, Montesquieu) and modern democracy.
section-91: In Book V of 'Politics', Aristotle analysed revolutions (changes in constitution or rulers). General causes: the desire for equality (by the many, who feel unequally treated) and the desire for superiority (by the few who think they deserve more) - in short, disagreements about justice and inequality. Particular causes include insolence and greed of rulers, fear, contempt, disproportionate increase in some part of the state, election intrigues, neglect of small changes, dissimilarity of elements (different races), and foreign influence.

Ways to prevent revolution: maintaining the rule of law and respect for the constitution; preventing small violations; avoiding extremes of wealth and poverty and strengthening the middle class; educating citizens in the spirit of the constitution; short terms of office; not allowing anyone excessive power; honest administration; and giving offices based on merit. Aristotle also gave advice for preserving each type of constitution, and even described how tyrants maintain power. His analysis is considered one of the first systematic studies of political change.
section-92: Aristotle argued that slavery is natural: some people are by nature fitted to rule (masters, who possess reason) and others to be ruled (slaves, who can understand reason but cannot use it to govern themselves). The slave is 'a living tool' or 'animate instrument' of the household, and slavery benefits both master and slave. He distinguished natural slavery from legal or conventional slavery (such as prisoners of war), which he considered unjust if the enslaved were naturally free, especially if Greeks were enslaved.

He recommended that masters treat slaves humanely and that slaves be allowed to earn freedom. His theory reflected the Greek economy, which depended on slave labour, and Greek prejudices against 'barbarians'. It was later used to justify slavery in the Americas. Modern ideas of human equality, dignity and human rights (UDHR Article 4: 'No one shall be held in slavery') completely reject it.
section-93: Niccolò Machiavelli (1469-1527) was a Florentine diplomat and official. After the Medici returned to power (1512), he was dismissed, tortured and exiled to his farm, where he wrote 'The Prince' (1513, published 1532), dedicated to Lorenzo de' Medici, and 'Discourses on the First Ten Books of Livy' (on republics). He is called the 'father of modern political science' and the first modern political thinker because he separated politics from ethics and religion.

He argued that the ruler must be ready to act immorally when necessary for the security of the state - 'a prince who wishes to maintain himself must learn how not to be good' - and that the end (preserving the state) justifies the means (a phrase associated with him, though not his exact words). The prince should be both a 'fox' (to recognise traps) and a 'lion' (to frighten wolves); it is safer to be feared than loved if one cannot be both. He saw religion as useful for maintaining social order and unity (praising Roman religion), but criticised the Church for keeping Italy divided. 'Machiavellian' came to mean cunning and unscrupulous, but scholars note his realism and his patriotism (desire for a united Italy) and republicanism.
section-94: Machiavelli emphasised that the state's survival and power are the supreme goals. A strong state requires 'virtù' (the ability, energy and skill of the ruler to master circumstances) and luck ('fortuna'), which he compared to a river in flood - virtù builds dikes against it. He stressed that a state needs 'good laws and good arms', preferring a citizen army to mercenaries, whom he considered useless and dangerous.

He held a realistic view of human nature: people are 'ungrateful, fickle, liars and deceivers, fearful of danger and greedy for gain', so the ruler must use fear and force when necessary. He studied how principalities are acquired (by arms, fortune, crime or the favour of citizens) and maintained. In the 'Discourses', he praised the mixed constitution of the Roman Republic and the participation of citizens, showing that he valued liberty and republican government. He laid the foundation of the modern secular nation-state and of the concept of 'reason of state' (raison d'état).
section-95: Thomas Hobbes (1588-1679) wrote 'Leviathan' (1651) during the period of the English Civil War. He described the state of nature as a condition without government, in which people are equal in their ability to kill each other and driven by self-interest, fear and the desire for power. It is a 'war of all against all' in which life is 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short'. There is no justice, property or industry.

To escape this, people make a social contract with each other, agreeing to surrender all their rights (except the right of self-preservation) to a sovereign - one person or an assembly - who is not party to the contract. The sovereign is absolute, indivisible and unlimited; subjects cannot rebel (except if the sovereign threatens their lives), and the sovereign's laws define justice. The state, which he called the 'Leviathan' or 'mortal God', provides peace and security. Hobbes was the first to base the state on individual consent rather than divine right, but his conclusion supported absolutism. Critics note that his view of human nature is pessimistic and that his theory gives no protection against tyranny.
section-96: John Locke (1632-1704) wrote 'Two Treatises of Government' (1690), justifying the Glorious Revolution of 1688. He described the state of nature as a state of peace, goodwill and mutual assistance, governed by natural law (reason) under which people have natural rights to life, liberty and property ('estate'). However, it has inconveniences: there is no established law, no impartial judge and no power to enforce decisions.

So people make a social contract, giving up only the right to interpret and enforce natural law, to establish a civil society and a limited government that protects their rights. Government is based on consent (including tacit consent), the majority rules, and the legislature is supreme but limited by natural law. If the government violates the trust by violating rights, the people have the right to resist and replace it (right of revolution). Locke also argued that property arises when a person mixes their labour with nature, and he supported religious toleration ('A Letter Concerning Toleration', 1689). He is the 'father of liberalism', influencing the American Declaration of Independence and constitutional democracy.
section-97: Jean-Jacques Rousseau (1712-1778) wrote 'Discourse on the Origin of Inequality' (1755) and 'The Social Contract' (1762), which begins: 'Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains.' The state of nature was idyllic - the 'noble savage' lived in simple happiness, guided by self-love (amour de soi) and pity. Private property, civilisation and society corrupted people, creating inequality, vanity (amour-propre) and conflict.

The social contract: each person gives himself entirely to the community, placing himself under the supreme direction of the 'general will'; in return, each becomes an indivisible part of the whole. The general will is the will of the community aimed at the common good, different from the 'will of all' (the sum of private interests). Sovereignty belongs to the people and is inalienable, indivisible and infallible; it cannot be represented, so Rousseau favoured direct democracy. Obedience to the general will is true freedom ('whoever refuses to obey the general will shall be forced to be free'). He is the 'father of popular sovereignty' and inspired the French Revolution. Critics (Benjamin Constant, J. L. Talmon - 'totalitarian democracy') argue that the general will can justify tyranny, while others see him as a theorist of radical democracy and equality.
section-98: Jeremy Bentham (1748-1832), an English philosopher and legal reformer, wrote 'A Fragment on Government' (1776) and 'An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation' (1789). He began: 'Nature has placed mankind under the governance of two sovereign masters, pain and pleasure.' The principle of utility says that the right action is that which produces 'the greatest happiness of the greatest number'.

He proposed a 'felicific calculus' to measure pleasure and pain by intensity, duration, certainty, propinquity (nearness), fecundity, purity and extent. Bentham said 'quantity of pleasure being equal, pushpin is as good as poetry' - he made no distinction between higher and lower pleasures. He rejected natural rights ('nonsense upon stilts') and the social contract as fictions. He advocated legal and political reforms: codification of law, prison reform (the 'Panopticon' design), extension of suffrage, secret ballot, annual parliaments and a minimal but active state. Criticisms: pleasures cannot be measured; utilitarianism can justify sacrificing minorities; and it ignores rights and justice.
section-99: John Stuart Mill (1806-1873), son of James Mill and disciple of Bentham, revised utilitarianism by distinguishing higher (intellectual, moral) and lower (bodily) pleasures: 'It is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied; better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied.' In 'On Liberty' (1859), he defended the liberty of thought and expression, individuality and the 'harm principle': 'the only purpose for which power can be rightfully exercised over any member of a civilised community, against his will, is to prevent harm to others.' His own good is not a sufficient reason.

He distinguished self-regarding actions (which concern only the individual and should be free) from other-regarding actions (which affect others and may be regulated). He defended freedom of speech because (1) the suppressed opinion may be true; (2) even if false, it may contain part of the truth; (3) truth unchallenged becomes 'dead dogma'; and (4) debate strengthens understanding. He warned against the 'tyranny of the majority' and social conformity. Criticisms: the distinction between self-regarding and other-regarding actions is difficult to draw, and his liberty was not for 'backward' societies, reflecting colonial attitudes (he worked for the East India Company).
section-100: In 'Considerations on Representative Government' (1861), Mill argued that the ideally best form of government is representative government, because it protects people's interests and develops their intellectual and moral qualities through participation. He supported extending the franchise to all adults, including women ('The Subjection of Women', 1869), and as an MP (1865-1868) he proposed an amendment for women's suffrage.

However, to protect against the tyranny of the majority and the ignorance of the masses, he proposed: plural voting (more votes for the educated); excluding those who could not read, write and do basic arithmetic or who received poor relief; proportional representation (Thomas Hare's system) to protect minorities; open rather than secret ballot (to encourage public responsibility); a strong second chamber; and a legislative commission of experts to draft laws. Mill is regarded as a bridge between classical and modern liberalism, though his proposals for plural voting are considered elitist.
section-101: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel (1770-1831), a German idealist philosopher, wrote 'Phenomenology of Spirit' (1807) and 'Philosophy of Right' (1821). His dialectical method, often explained (though he did not use these exact terms) as thesis, antithesis and synthesis: every idea or situation (thesis) contains contradictions that give rise to its opposite (antithesis), and the conflict is resolved in a higher stage (synthesis), which becomes a new thesis. Change is thus progressive.

For Hegel, history is the progress of the 'Absolute Spirit' (Geist) or Reason realising itself, and the development of the consciousness of freedom: in the Oriental world, one person (the despot) was free; in the Greek and Roman world, some were free; and in the Germanic-Christian world, all are free. 'What is rational is actual and what is actual is rational.' His idealist dialectics influenced Marx, who 'turned Hegel upside down' by replacing ideas with matter.
section-102: Hegel saw ethical life (Sittlichkeit) as developing through three stages: the family (based on love and unity - thesis), civil society (based on individual self-interest, competition, the market and needs - antithesis) and the state (synthesis), which reconciles particular interests with the universal good. The state is 'the march of God on earth', 'the actuality of the ethical idea' and 'the realisation of freedom'. Individuals find true freedom by identifying with the rational state.

He favoured a constitutional monarchy with a bureaucracy (the 'universal class') and representation of estates. He saw war as sometimes necessary to maintain the health of nations. Critics (Karl Popper, Bertrand Russell) argued that Hegel glorified the state and influenced totalitarianism (fascism), while defenders (Shlomo Avineri, Charles Taylor) see him as a theorist of a rational, constitutional state. He influenced both the right (state worship) and the left (Marx and the Young Hegelians).
section-103: Dialectical materialism (a term used by later Marxists, especially Plekhanov and Engels) combines Hegel's dialectical method with materialism (Feuerbach): matter, not mind or ideas, is the primary reality; consciousness and ideas reflect material conditions. Marx said, 'It is not the consciousness of men that determines their being, but, on the contrary, their social being that determines their consciousness.'

Engels ('Dialectics of Nature', 'Anti-Dühring') stated three laws of dialectics: (1) the unity and struggle of opposites (contradictions within things cause change); (2) the transformation of quantity into quality (gradual changes lead to sudden qualitative change, like water becoming steam); and (3) the negation of the negation (development occurs in a spiral, preserving elements of earlier stages). Marx thus stood Hegel 'on his feet'. Critics argue that the laws are vague and cannot be scientifically tested (Popper).
section-104: Historical materialism applies dialectical materialism to society and history. In the Preface to 'A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy' (1859), Marx explained that the economic structure or 'base' - consisting of the forces of production (tools, technology, labour) and relations of production (ownership and class relations) - determines the 'superstructure' of law, politics, religion, art and philosophy.

History passes through stages based on modes of production: primitive communism (no private property, no classes), slavery (masters and slaves), feudalism (lords and serfs), capitalism (bourgeoisie and proletariat), and the future socialism and communism. Change occurs when the forces of production come into conflict with the relations of production, leading to class struggle and revolution. Criticisms: economic determinism ignores the independent role of ideas, religion, culture and individuals (Max Weber's 'Protestant Ethic' argued that ideas influenced capitalism); history has not followed the predicted stages; and later Marxists (Gramsci, Althusser) gave more importance to the superstructure.
section-105: Marx argued that revolution occurs when the contradictions between the forces and relations of production become acute. Under capitalism, contradictions include the concentration of wealth in fewer hands, the impoverishment and growing numbers of workers (the 'immiseration' of the proletariat), recurring economic crises of overproduction and the alienation of workers. Workers would develop class consciousness, from a 'class in itself' to a 'class for itself', organise and overthrow capitalism through revolution, possibly violent ('Workers of the world, unite! You have nothing to lose but your chains').

After the revolution, the 'dictatorship of the proletariat' would abolish private property in the means of production and suppress the bourgeoisie. This socialist stage ('from each according to his ability, to each according to his work') would lead to communism, a classless, stateless society ('from each according to his ability, to each according to his needs'), in which the state would 'wither away' (Engels). Marx expected revolution in advanced capitalist countries like England and Germany, but it happened in less developed Russia (1917) and China (1949), which Lenin and Mao explained through their own theories.
section-106: 'The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles' (Communist Manifesto, 1848). Classes are defined by their relation to the means of production: owners and non-owners. In each era, an exploiting class confronts an exploited class - freeman and slave, patrician and plebeian, lord and serf, guild-master and journeyman, and in capitalism, the bourgeoisie and the proletariat. Class interests are opposed and irreconcilable.

Capitalism simplifies class antagonisms into two great classes, as the middle classes (small producers, artisans) sink into the proletariat. The state, law and ideology serve the ruling class ('the ideas of the ruling class are in every epoch the ruling ideas'). Class struggle ends only with the abolition of classes under communism. Criticisms: modern societies have a large middle class, the welfare state and trade unions have improved workers' conditions, and other identities (nation, religion, race, gender) often matter more than class. Max Weber argued that stratification involves class, status and party.
section-107: In 'Capital' (Das Kapital, Volume I, 1867), Marx developed the labour theory of value (from Adam Smith and David Ricardo): the value of a commodity is determined by the socially necessary labour time required to produce it. Labour power is a special commodity because it can produce more value than its own value (the cost of the worker's subsistence). The capitalist buys labour power for wages equal to its value, but makes the worker work longer than needed to produce that value.

For example, if a worker produces the value of his daily wage in six hours but works twelve, the value produced in the extra six hours is 'surplus value', appropriated by the capitalist as profit. This is the source of exploitation. Capitalists increase surplus value by lengthening the working day (absolute surplus value) or increasing productivity through machinery (relative surplus value). Marx predicted that competition and mechanisation would lead to a falling rate of profit and crises. Critics (Böhm-Bawerk, marginalist economists) argue that value depends on utility and demand, and that capital, risk and entrepreneurship also create value.
section-109: Plato's theory of justice: rejecting conventional views (Cephalus, Polemarchus, Thrasymachus, Glaucon), Plato defined justice as each class performing its proper function - rulers (reason, wisdom), auxiliaries (spirit, courage) and producers (appetite, temperance) - in harmony. Justice is the principle of specialisation and non-interference, both in the soul and the state. It is a moral and functional concept rather than legal.

Education and communism: state-controlled education for men and women, from music and gymnastics to mathematics and dialectics, selects and trains philosopher-rulers; communism of property and family for the guardian classes prevents corruption and promotes unity. Ideal state: rule of philosopher-kings who know the 'Form of the Good', three classes based on aptitude (myth of metals), equality of women, and rule by knowledge rather than law.

Evaluation: Plato's contributions include the idea that rulers must be qualified and devoted to the public good, the importance of education, equality of women (revolutionary for his time) and the search for a just society. Criticisms: authoritarianism (Popper), neglect of individual liberty and consent, rigid class division, censorship, lack of checks on rulers, utopianism and the exclusion of producers from political life. In 'The Laws', Plato himself moved towards a more practical state based on law. His work remains foundational to Western political philosophy.
section-110: Aristotle's method was empirical and comparative, based on the study of 158 constitutions; he is called the father of Political Science. Man is a 'political animal', and the state (polis) exists 'for the sake of the good life'. Classification of constitutions: by number of rulers and purpose - monarchy/tyranny, aristocracy/oligarchy, polity/democracy - with a cycle of change. Best practicable state: polity, a mixed constitution with a large middle class and the golden mean, rule of law and moderate citizenship qualifications.

Revolution: caused by disputes over justice and inequality (the many want equality, the few want superiority), and particular causes such as insolence, fear, contempt, disproportionate growth of classes and neglect of small changes; prevented by rule of law, moderation, strong middle class, education in the constitution and honest administration. Slavery: Aristotle defended natural slavery - some are by nature rulers and others slaves - while recommending humane treatment; he also considered women inferior to men and denied citizenship to labourers.

Evaluation: Aristotle's realism, empiricism and emphasis on the middle class, rule of law and mixed constitution influenced later thinkers (Polybius, Aquinas, Montesquieu, the US founders). His views on slavery and women reflect the prejudices of his society and are rejected by modern principles of equality. Comparing Plato and Aristotle: Plato was idealist, deductive and favoured rule by philosophers; Aristotle was realist, inductive and favoured rule of law and a practical constitution - Raphael's painting 'The School of Athens' shows Plato pointing upward and Aristotle pointing to the earth.
section-111: Background: Renaissance Italy was divided into city-states and principalities, often controlled by foreign powers (France, Spain) and the Papacy. Machiavelli, a patriot, wanted a strong ruler to unify Italy and expel foreigners (the last chapter of The Prince is an 'Exhortation to liberate Italy from the barbarians'). He used historical examples (ancient Rome, Cesare Borgia) and observation rather than abstract principles.

Separation of politics from ethics and religion: the ruler should follow 'reason of state' - doing whatever is necessary to preserve the state, even if immoral (deception, cruelty used wisely). He distinguished private morality from public morality; a ruler should appear virtuous but be willing to act otherwise. Religion is useful as a tool for unity and obedience, but the Church had corrupted Italy. Human nature is selfish, so rulers must use fear; 'virtù' and 'fortuna'; good laws and good arms (a citizen militia).

Evaluation: Machiavelli is the father of modern political science and realism because he described politics as it is, not as it should be. He contributed to the concept of the secular sovereign state and nationalism. Critics condemned him as immoral ('Old Nick'); defenders (Isaiah Berlin) argue that he recognised the conflict between different moral systems - Christian virtue and civic virtue. His 'Discourses' show his admiration for republican liberty and citizen participation.
section-112: Hobbes ('Leviathan', 1651): pessimistic view of human nature (selfish, fearful, power-seeking); state of nature as war of all against all ('nasty, brutish and short'); contract among individuals to surrender all rights to an absolute sovereign who is not a party to the contract; sovereign's power is unlimited and indivisible; no right of rebellion except self-preservation. Contribution: the state is based on consent and created for security; individualism; legal sovereignty. Criticism: absolutism, pessimism.

Locke ('Two Treatises', 1690): human nature is rational and sociable; the state of nature is peaceful, governed by natural law, with natural rights to life, liberty and property, but with inconveniences; the contract creates a limited government based on consent and trust; government protects natural rights; the legislature is supreme but limited; and people have a right to resist and change a government that violates their rights. Contribution: liberalism, constitutionalism, limited government, popular consent and the right of revolution. Criticism: defence of property can justify inequality; tacit consent is vague.

Rousseau ('The Social Contract', 1762): man is naturally good, corrupted by society and property; the contract involves total alienation of each to the community, creating a collective body guided by the general will; sovereignty belongs to the people, is inalienable and indivisible, and cannot be represented; true freedom is obedience to self-prescribed law. Contribution: popular sovereignty, democracy and equality; inspiration for the French Revolution. Criticism: the general will is vague and may justify tyranny. Comparison: Hobbes leads to absolute monarchy, Locke to limited constitutional government, and Rousseau to popular sovereignty and direct democracy.
section-113: Bentham: the principle of utility ('greatest happiness of the greatest number'); human behaviour governed by pleasure and pain; felicific calculus; no qualitative distinction between pleasures; rejection of natural rights and the social contract; law as the command of the sovereign; reforms - codification, prison reform (Panopticon), democratic reforms (extension of suffrage, secret ballot), and a state that promotes happiness through legislation. Criticisms: pleasures cannot be measured; majority happiness may sacrifice minorities; it ignores justice and rights.

J. S. Mill: qualitative utilitarianism (higher and lower pleasures); 'On Liberty' (1859) - harm principle, freedom of thought and expression, individuality and the danger of social tyranny; representative government as the best form ('Considerations on Representative Government', 1861), with universal suffrage including women, but plural voting for the educated, proportional representation and safeguards against majority tyranny; 'The Subjection of Women' (1869) argued for gender equality. Mill moved from classical to modern liberalism, recognising a role for the state in education and labour.

Evaluation: Bentham and Mill shaped liberal and utilitarian thought, legal reform and democratic institutions in Britain and beyond, including India (Bentham's influence on codification - the Indian Penal Code of 1860, drafted by Macaulay, reflects utilitarian ideas; Mill worked for the East India Company). Mill's defence of liberty remains central to debates on free speech, while his elitism and colonial views are criticised.
section-114: Hegel's dialectics: reality and history develop through contradictions - thesis, antithesis and synthesis - as the 'World Spirit' (Geist) realises itself and achieves self-consciousness and freedom. History is the progress of freedom: from one free (Oriental despotism) to some free (Greek and Roman) to all free (the Germanic-Christian world). 'The owl of Minerva spreads its wings only with the falling of the dusk' - philosophy understands an era only when it is ending.

Theory of the state: ethical life develops through the family (unity based on love), civil society (the system of needs, market, competition, administration of justice and corporations) and the state (the synthesis, in which the universal and particular are reconciled). The state is the 'actuality of the ethical idea', 'the march of God on earth', an end in itself rather than a means for individuals. Hegel favoured constitutional monarchy, bureaucracy as the universal class and representation through estates.

Evaluation: Hegel contributed the dialectical method, a historical understanding of institutions and the idea of the state as an ethical community. Critics such as Popper and Russell said his glorification of the state led to authoritarianism and nationalism (German and Italian fascism), and Marx criticised his idealism. Others argue that Hegel's state is a constitutional, rational one protecting freedom. His influence extends to Marxism, existentialism, critical theory and communitarianism.
section-115: Dialectical and historical materialism: Marx combined Hegel's dialectics with materialism; the economic base (forces and relations of production) determines the superstructure (law, politics, ideology); history moves through modes of production - primitive communism, slavery, feudalism, capitalism, socialism and communism - driven by contradictions between forces and relations of production. Class struggle: history is a history of class struggles; in capitalism, between the bourgeoisie and the proletariat; the state is an instrument of class domination.

Surplus value and exploitation: according to the labour theory of value, workers produce more value than they receive as wages; the difference (surplus value) is appropriated by capitalists as profit, which is the basis of exploitation. Capitalism also produces alienation of workers from their product, labour, fellow workers and their human essence ('Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts', 1844). Revolution: capitalist contradictions (crises, concentration of capital, growing proletariat and class consciousness) lead to a proletarian revolution, the dictatorship of the proletariat, socialism and finally a classless, stateless communist society.

Evaluation: Marx's analysis of capitalism, class, exploitation and ideology has deeply influenced social science and political movements (Russian, Chinese, Cuban and Vietnamese revolutions; socialist and labour parties; the welfare state). Criticisms: economic determinism; predictions of proletarian revolution in advanced capitalist countries failed; capitalism adapted through reforms; communist states became authoritarian; the labour theory of value is disputed; and the neglect of nationalism, religion, gender and individual rights. Neo-Marxists (Gramsci, the Frankfurt School, Althusser) revised Marx's ideas, and his critique remains relevant in debates on inequality and globalisation.
section-118: International organisations are formal institutions created by agreement among states (intergovernmental organisations, IGOs - such as the UN, WTO, IMF, ASEAN, SAARC, African Union, NATO) or by private actors (international NGOs - such as Amnesty International, the International Committee of the Red Cross, Greenpeace). IGOs have a permanent structure, members, rules and functions. Early examples include the Concert of Europe (1815), international river commissions (the Rhine, 1815), the International Telegraph Union (1865) and the Universal Postal Union (1874). The League of Nations (1920) was the first general political organisation.

Functions: providing a forum for negotiation, making rules and norms, maintaining peace and security, promoting economic and social cooperation, providing services (health, development aid) and monitoring compliance. Theories: realists see international organisations as tools of powerful states; liberal institutionalists see them as facilitating cooperation by reducing transaction costs and building trust; constructivists see them as shaping norms and identities; and functionalists (David Mitrany, 'A Working Peace System', 1943) see technical cooperation leading to peace.
section-119: Steps leading to the UN: the London Declaration (June 1941); the Atlantic Charter (14 August 1941) of Roosevelt and Churchill; the Declaration by United Nations (1 January 1942), signed by 26 nations fighting the Axis (the name 'United Nations' was coined by Roosevelt); the Moscow Declaration (October 1943) calling for a general international organisation; the Tehran Conference (1943); the Dumbarton Oaks Conference (August-October 1944) in Washington, where the USA, UK, USSR and China drafted proposals; and the Yalta Conference (February 1945), which agreed on Security Council voting (the veto).

The United Nations Conference on International Organization (San Francisco, 25 April - 26 June 1945) was attended by 50 countries, which signed the Charter on 26 June 1945 (Poland signed later as the 51st original member). The UN came into existence on 24 October 1945 (UN Day) after ratification by the five permanent members and a majority of signatories. India was a founding member, signing the Charter in 1945 even before independence. The UN headquarters is in New York (land donated by John D. Rockefeller Jr.); other offices are in Geneva, Vienna and Nairobi. The UN replaced the League of Nations, which was formally dissolved in 1946.
section-120: The UN Charter has a Preamble and 111 articles in 19 chapters. The Preamble begins: 'We the peoples of the United Nations determined to save succeeding generations from the scourge of war, which twice in our lifetime has brought untold sorrow to mankind, and to reaffirm faith in fundamental human rights, in the dignity and worth of the human person, in the equal rights of men and women and of nations large and small...'

Important chapters: I (Purposes and Principles), III (Organs), IV-V (General Assembly and Security Council), VI (Pacific Settlement of Disputes), VII (Action with respect to Threats to the Peace, Breaches of the Peace and Acts of Aggression - enforcement measures, Articles 39-51, including Article 51 on the right of self-defence), VIII (Regional Arrangements), IX-X (International Economic and Social Cooperation, ECOSOC), XI-XIII (Non-Self-Governing Territories and Trusteeship), XIV (International Court of Justice) and XV (Secretariat). Article 103 makes Charter obligations prevail over other treaties. Amendment (Article 108) requires a two-thirds vote of the General Assembly and ratification by two-thirds of members, including all five permanent members. The Charter has been amended a few times (enlarging the Security Council from 11 to 15 in 1965 and ECOSOC from 18 to 27 and then 54).
section-121: Article 1 lists the purposes: (1) to maintain international peace and security, taking effective collective measures to prevent and remove threats to peace and suppress acts of aggression, and to settle disputes by peaceful means in conformity with justice and international law; (2) to develop friendly relations among nations based on respect for the principle of equal rights and self-determination of peoples; (3) to achieve international cooperation in solving international problems of an economic, social, cultural or humanitarian character, and in promoting respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms for all without distinction as to race, sex, language or religion; and (4) to be a centre for harmonising the actions of nations in attaining these common ends.

These objectives have expanded in practice to include peacekeeping, decolonisation, development (the Millennium Development Goals, 2000-2015, and the Sustainable Development Goals, 2015-2030, with 17 goals), environmental protection (climate change conferences under the UNFCCC, the Paris Agreement 2015), humanitarian assistance, disarmament and counter-terrorism.
section-122: Article 2 lists seven principles: (1) sovereign equality of all members; (2) members shall fulfil in good faith the obligations of the Charter; (3) members shall settle their disputes by peaceful means; (4) members shall refrain from the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state; (5) members shall give the UN every assistance in any action it takes and refrain from assisting any state against which the UN is taking preventive or enforcement action; (6) the UN shall ensure that non-member states act in accordance with these principles as necessary for peace; and (7) the UN shall not intervene in matters essentially within the domestic jurisdiction of any state, except for enforcement measures under Chapter VII.

These principles reflect the Westphalian ideas of sovereignty and non-intervention, combined with collective security. Tensions have arisen between non-intervention and the protection of human rights, leading to debates on humanitarian intervention and the 'Responsibility to Protect' (2005). Violations, such as the US-led invasion of Iraq (2003) and Russia's invasion of Ukraine (2022), have raised questions about the UN's effectiveness.
section-123: The General Assembly (Chapter IV, Articles 9-22) consists of all 193 member states, each with one vote (sovereign equality). It meets in regular annual sessions from September (the 'general debate' of world leaders) and in special and emergency special sessions. It elects a President each year (Vijaya Lakshmi Pandit of India was the first woman President of the General Assembly, 1953). Decisions on important questions (peace and security, admission of members, budget, elections to councils) require a two-thirds majority; other questions a simple majority.

Functions: deliberative (it can discuss any matter within the scope of the Charter and make recommendations - except on disputes being dealt with by the Security Council, Article 12); financial (approves the UN budget and members' contributions); elective (elects the non-permanent members of the Security Council, members of ECOSOC and, with the Security Council, judges of the ICJ; appoints the Secretary-General on the Council's recommendation; admits new members on the Council's recommendation); and constituent (participates in Charter amendments). The 'Uniting for Peace' Resolution (1950) allows the General Assembly to recommend collective action when the Security Council is deadlocked by the veto. Its resolutions are not legally binding (except on internal matters), but carry moral weight; it has been called 'the town meeting of the world'.
section-124: The Security Council (Chapter V, Articles 23-32) has 15 members: five permanent members (P5) - China, France, Russia (successor to the USSR since 1991), the United Kingdom and the United States - and ten non-permanent members elected by the General Assembly for two-year terms (five each year) on a regional basis; they cannot be immediately re-elected. India has been a non-permanent member eight times, most recently in 2021-2022. The presidency rotates monthly.

Voting (Article 27): procedural matters require nine affirmative votes; substantive matters require nine votes including the concurring votes of all permanent members - this is the 'veto' (abstention by a permanent member is not considered a veto by practice). The Soviet Union/Russia and the USA have used the veto most often. Powers: investigating disputes, recommending methods of settlement (Chapter VI), determining threats to peace and deciding on enforcement measures - economic sanctions, arms embargoes, and military action (Chapter VII, Articles 41-42), establishing peacekeeping operations, recommending admission of members and the appointment of the Secretary-General, and electing ICJ judges with the General Assembly. Its decisions are binding on all members (Article 25).
section-125: ECOSOC (Chapter X, Articles 61-72) has 54 members elected by the General Assembly for three-year terms (18 each year), with regional distribution. It coordinates the economic, social, humanitarian and environmental work of the UN, its specialised agencies, funds and programmes, and functional and regional commissions (such as the Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific, ESCAP, in Bangkok, and the Commission on the Status of Women).

Functions: making studies and reports on international economic, social, cultural, educational and health matters; making recommendations to the General Assembly, members and specialised agencies; promoting respect for human rights; preparing draft conventions; calling international conferences; coordinating specialised agencies through agreements; and consulting with NGOs (over 5,000 NGOs have consultative status). It holds the High-Level Political Forum on Sustainable Development, which reviews progress on the SDGs. Critics say it is too large and has limited influence compared with institutions like the IMF and World Bank.
section-126: The Secretariat (Chapter XV, Articles 97-101) is the administrative organ, with about 37,000 international civil servants worldwide, who must be independent and not take instructions from any government (Article 100). It is headed by the Secretary-General, appointed by the General Assembly on the recommendation of the Security Council (subject to veto) for a five-year term, renewable once by convention.

The Secretary-General is the 'chief administrative officer' (Article 97), attends meetings of the main organs, presents the annual report, may bring to the Security Council's attention any matter that threatens peace (Article 99), uses 'good offices' for mediation, and acts as the UN's spokesperson. Secretaries-General: Trygve Lie (Norway, 1946-1952), Dag Hammarskjöld (Sweden, 1953-1961, died in a plane crash in Congo, posthumous Nobel Peace Prize), U Thant (Burma, 1961-1971), Kurt Waldheim (Austria), Javier Pérez de Cuéllar (Peru), Boutros Boutros-Ghali (Egypt, 'An Agenda for Peace', 1992), Kofi Annan (Ghana, 1997-2006, Nobel Peace Prize 2001), Ban Ki-moon (South Korea, 2007-2016) and António Guterres (Portugal, since 2017). No woman has yet held the post.
section-127: The International Court of Justice (Chapter XIV and the ICJ Statute), located at the Peace Palace in The Hague, Netherlands, succeeded the Permanent Court of International Justice of the League. It has 15 judges elected for nine-year terms by absolute majorities in both the General Assembly and the Security Council, with no two judges from the same country; one-third are elected every three years. Indian judges have included B. N. Rau, Nagendra Singh (President, 1985-1988), R. S. Pathak and Dalveer Bhandari (since 2012).

Jurisdiction: contentious cases between states that consent to its jurisdiction (by special agreement, treaty clauses or optional declarations under Article 36(2)); only states can be parties. Its judgements are binding on the parties; if a party fails to comply, the other may approach the Security Council (Article 94). Advisory opinions are given on legal questions referred by UN organs and agencies (for example, on the legality of nuclear weapons, 1996, the Israeli wall, 2004, Kosovo's declaration of independence, 2010, and Israel's occupation of Palestinian territories, 2024). India's cases include the Kulbhushan Jadhav case against Pakistan (2017-2019), in which the ICJ ruled in India's favour on consular access. Limitations: consent-based jurisdiction and lack of enforcement.
section-128: The ILO was established in 1919 under the Treaty of Versailles, became the first specialised agency of the UN in 1946, and is headquartered in Geneva. It has a unique tripartite structure: governments, employers and workers are represented in its General Conference (the International Labour Conference), the Governing Body and other organs. It won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1969. India is a founding member.

Functions: setting international labour standards through conventions and recommendations (about 190 conventions on freedom of association, forced labour, child labour - Conventions 138 and 182, discrimination, working hours, safety and social security); supervising their application; providing technical assistance; promoting the 'Decent Work Agenda' (employment, rights at work, social protection and social dialogue); research and statistics; and the Declaration on Fundamental Principles and Rights at Work (1998), covering freedom of association, elimination of forced labour, abolition of child labour, elimination of discrimination and (since 2022) a safe and healthy working environment.
section-129: UNESCO (United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization) was founded on 16 November 1945, with headquarters in Paris. Its constitution states: 'Since wars begin in the minds of men, it is in the minds of men that the defences of peace must be constructed.' It has about 194 member states (the USA has withdrawn and rejoined several times, most recently rejoining in 2023 and announcing withdrawal again in 2025).

Activities: promoting education for all (literacy, quality education, SDG 4); science (the Man and the Biosphere programme, oceanography, water resources); culture - the World Heritage Convention (1972), under which over 1,100 sites are listed (India has over 40, including the Taj Mahal, Kaziranga, Manas, and the Ahom maidams of Charaideo, inscribed in 2024); the Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage (2003; India's elements include yoga, Kumbh Mela, Durga Puja in Kolkata and Garba); communication and information (press freedom, World Press Freedom Day); and protection of cultural property in armed conflict.
section-130: The World Health Organization was established on 7 April 1948 (World Health Day), with headquarters in Geneva. Its constitution defines health as 'a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity'. Its governing body is the World Health Assembly; it has six regional offices (South-East Asia's is in New Delhi).

Achievements: eradication of smallpox (declared in 1980); near-eradication of polio (India was declared polio-free in 2014); campaigns against malaria, tuberculosis, HIV/AIDS, leprosy and neglected tropical diseases; the Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (2003); International Health Regulations (2005); setting standards for medicines and vaccines (the Essential Medicines List); and coordinating responses to epidemics (SARS 2003, Ebola 2014-2016, COVID-19 pandemic declared in March 2020, with the COVAX initiative for vaccine distribution). It has been criticised for slow responses and dependence on voluntary donor funding; the USA announced its withdrawal in 2025. A Pandemic Agreement was adopted by the World Health Assembly in 2025.
section-131: UNICEF was created by the General Assembly on 11 December 1946 as the United Nations International Children's Emergency Fund, to provide emergency food and health care to children in countries devastated by the Second World War. In 1953, it became a permanent part of the UN and its name was shortened to the United Nations Children's Fund (keeping the acronym). Headquarters: New York. It won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1965. It is funded entirely by voluntary contributions from governments and private donors.

Activities: child survival and health (immunisation, oral rehydration therapy, nutrition, breastfeeding promotion), education (especially for girls), water, sanitation and hygiene, child protection (against violence, exploitation, child labour, child marriage and recruitment as soldiers), emergency relief during conflicts and disasters, and advocacy for the Convention on the Rights of the Child. It publishes 'The State of the World's Children' report. In India, it works with the government on immunisation, nutrition (ICDS), sanitation (Swachh Bharat) and education.
section-132: UNDP was established in 1965 by merging the Expanded Programme of Technical Assistance (1949) and the UN Special Fund (1958). Headquarters: New York. It works in about 170 countries and territories to eradicate poverty, reduce inequalities and build resilience, focusing on sustainable development, democratic governance and peacebuilding, and climate and disaster resilience. It coordinates the UN's work on the Sustainable Development Goals at the country level.

Since 1990, UNDP has published the annual Human Development Report, created by Pakistani economist Mahbub ul Haq with Amartya Sen. Its Human Development Index (HDI) measures development using life expectancy, education (mean and expected years of schooling) and income (GNI per capita), moving beyond GDP. Other indices include the Gender Development Index, Gender Inequality Index and Multidimensional Poverty Index (with Oxford's OPHI). India ranked 134th out of 193 countries in the 2023-2024 HDR. The 1994 Human Development Report introduced the concept of 'human security'.
section-133: UNEP was established in 1972 following the Stockholm Conference on the Human Environment. Its headquarters is in Nairobi, Kenya - the first UN agency headquartered in a developing country. It is the leading global environmental authority that sets the environmental agenda and promotes the environmental dimension of sustainable development. Its governing body is the UN Environment Assembly (since 2012, with universal membership).

Achievements: it facilitated major environmental agreements - the Vienna Convention (1985) and Montreal Protocol (1987) on protecting the ozone layer (considered the most successful environmental treaty; the Kigali Amendment, 2016, phases down HFCs), the Basel Convention (1989) on hazardous waste, the Convention on Biological Diversity (1992), the Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants (2001) and the Minamata Convention on Mercury (2013). It co-founded the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC, 1988) with the World Meteorological Organization; the IPCC shared the Nobel Peace Prize in 2007. It publishes the Global Environment Outlook and Emissions Gap reports, and leads World Environment Day (5 June). Negotiations for a global plastics treaty began in 2022.
section-134: After the Cold War, the Security Council became more active: it authorised the Gulf War (1991) against Iraq's invasion of Kuwait; the number of peacekeeping operations increased greatly (in Cambodia, Mozambique, Namibia, El Salvador), and peacekeeping became multidimensional (supervising elections, protecting civilians, building institutions). Boutros-Ghali's 'An Agenda for Peace' (1992) proposed preventive diplomacy, peacemaking, peacekeeping and post-conflict peacebuilding.

However, failures in Somalia (1993), Rwanda (the 1994 genocide, when UN forces were withdrawn) and Bosnia (the Srebrenica massacre, 1995) led to criticism. NATO's intervention in Kosovo (1999) and the US-led invasion of Iraq (2003) occurred without Security Council authorisation. New developments include international criminal tribunals and the ICC, the Millennium Declaration (2000) and MDGs, the Responsibility to Protect (2005), the Human Rights Council and Peacebuilding Commission (2005-2006), the SDGs (2015), the Paris Agreement (2015) and counter-terrorism committees. Renewed great power rivalry (Syria, Ukraine, Gaza) has again led to deadlock in the Security Council. India is one of the largest contributors of troops to UN peacekeeping, with over 2.5 lakh personnel having served in about 50 missions.
section-135: Reform proposals cover: (1) the Security Council - membership, representation and the veto; (2) the General Assembly - revitalisation to make it more effective; (3) ECOSOC - making it more relevant to economic governance; (4) the Secretariat - management reform, efficiency, accountability and transparency (Kofi Annan's 'In Larger Freedom', 2005); (5) peacekeeping - better mandates, resources and protection of civilians (the Brahimi Report, 2000); (6) human rights machinery - the Human Rights Council replaced the Commission (2006); and (7) finance - timely payment of contributions and reducing dependence on a few donors (the USA contributes the largest share, about 22 percent of the regular budget).

Other ideas include greater role for regional organisations, partnership with civil society and the private sector, gender parity, and selection of the Secretary-General through a more transparent process (introduced in 2016 with public hearings of candidates). The 'Pact for the Future' adopted at the Summit of the Future (September 2024) committed to reforming the Security Council and international financial architecture.
section-136: The Security Council reflects the power structure of 1945: the five permanent members are the victors of the Second World War, while Africa and Latin America have no permanent seats and Asia has only China. Membership of the UN has increased from 51 to 193, but the Council expanded only once (in 1965, from 11 to 15). Issues include the categories of membership (permanent and non-permanent), the question of the veto (abolition, restriction or extension to new members), regional representation, the size of an enlarged Council, working methods and the relationship with the General Assembly.

Groups and proposals: the G4 (India, Brazil, Germany and Japan) seek permanent seats and support each other's claims; the African Union's Ezulwini Consensus (2005) demands two permanent seats with veto and five non-permanent seats for Africa; the 'Uniting for Consensus' group (Italy, Pakistan, Argentina, South Korea, Mexico and others) opposes new permanent members and favours more non-permanent seats. Intergovernmental Negotiations have been held since 2009 without agreement. India's claim is based on its population, democracy, economy, contributions to peacekeeping and role in the developing world; several P5 members (the USA, UK, France, Russia) have expressed support, while China has not. Amendment requires two-thirds of members and the approval of all P5, making reform very difficult.
section-138: Background: the failure of the League of Nations (lack of US membership, unanimity rule, weak sanctions, failure against Japan, Italy and Germany) and the devastation of the Second World War convinced the Allies of the need for a stronger organisation. Stages: the Atlantic Charter (1941), the Declaration by United Nations (1942), the Moscow Declaration (1943), Dumbarton Oaks (1944), Yalta (1945), and the San Francisco Conference (April-June 1945), where 50 nations signed the Charter on 26 June 1945. The UN came into existence on 24 October 1945.

Charter: Preamble ('We the peoples of the United Nations...'), 111 articles in 19 chapters. Purposes (Article 1): international peace and security, friendly relations based on equal rights and self-determination, international cooperation in economic, social, cultural and humanitarian matters and human rights, and harmonising actions of nations. Principles (Article 2): sovereign equality, good faith fulfilment of obligations, peaceful settlement of disputes, non-use of force, assistance to UN actions, ensuring non-members follow principles, and non-intervention in domestic affairs.

Development: membership grew from 51 to 193 with decolonisation and the breakup of the USSR and Yugoslavia; the UN's activities expanded from security to development, human rights, environment, health and humanitarian relief through specialised agencies, funds and programmes. Differences from the League: universal membership, broader functions, stronger enforcement powers in Chapter VII, the veto to keep great powers involved, and peacekeeping. The Charter remains the constitutional framework of the international order.
section-139: General Assembly: all 193 members with one vote each; annual sessions; two-thirds majority for important questions; functions - deliberative, supervisory (receives reports from other organs), financial (budget), elective (non-permanent Security Council members, ECOSOC, ICJ judges with the Council, the Secretary-General on recommendation) and constituent (Charter amendments). Its resolutions are recommendations, not binding, but express world opinion; important declarations include the UDHR (1948), the Declaration on Decolonisation (1960), the NIEO (1974), and the SDGs (2015). The Uniting for Peace Resolution (1950) increased its role when the Council is deadlocked. It works through six main committees.

Security Council: 15 members (P5 with veto, ten elected for two years); primary responsibility for peace and security (Article 24); decisions binding on members (Article 25); powers under Chapter VI (peaceful settlement - investigation, mediation, recommendations) and Chapter VII (determining threats to peace, sanctions, military action); establishing peacekeeping missions, sanctions committees and international tribunals; and recommending new members and the Secretary-General. Achievements: Korea (1950), Suez (1956, first peacekeeping force UNEF), Congo (1960), Gulf War (1991), East Timor (1999). Failures: Cold War paralysis, Rwanda (1994), Srebrenica (1995), Syria, Ukraine and Gaza due to vetoes.

Comparison: the General Assembly represents the democratic principle of sovereign equality and broad deliberation; the Security Council represents the realist principle of great power responsibility and concentrated authority for security. The tension between the two - and between the veto and the equality of states - is at the heart of debates on UN reform.
section-140: ECOSOC: 54 members elected for three years; coordinates the economic, social, humanitarian and environmental work of the UN; supervises functional and regional commissions; conducts studies and makes recommendations; negotiates agreements with specialised agencies; consults NGOs; holds the High-Level Political Forum on the SDGs. Its role is important for development cooperation, though it is often overshadowed by the Bretton Woods institutions (IMF, World Bank) and the G20.

Secretariat: the administrative organ with international civil servants; headed by the Secretary-General, appointed for five years by the General Assembly on the Security Council's recommendation; functions - administration, implementing decisions, preparing reports and budgets, mediation ('good offices'), bringing threats to peace to the Council's attention (Article 99), and representing the UN. The Secretary-General's influence depends on personality and political circumstances (Hammarskjöld and Annan were particularly active).

International Court of Justice: 15 judges elected for nine years; located in The Hague; contentious jurisdiction (between consenting states, binding judgements) and advisory jurisdiction (opinions for UN organs and agencies). Notable cases: Corfu Channel (1949), Nicaragua v. USA (1986), the Bosnia genocide case (2007), Kulbhushan Jadhav (India v. Pakistan, 2019), and South Africa's case against Israel on the Genocide Convention (provisional measures, 2024). Limitations: jurisdiction depends on consent; enforcement relies on the Security Council. The Trusteeship Council suspended operations in 1994 after the last trust territory (Palau) became independent.
section-141: ILO (1919; UN specialised agency from 1946; Geneva): unique tripartite structure of governments, employers and workers; sets international labour standards through conventions and recommendations; supervises their implementation; promotes the Decent Work Agenda and social justice; provides technical assistance; Nobel Peace Prize (1969). Its work has helped establish norms on working hours, minimum wages, social security, freedom of association, and the elimination of forced and child labour.

UNESCO (1945; Paris): promotes cooperation in education (literacy, Education for All, SDG 4), natural sciences, social and human sciences, culture (World Heritage sites, intangible heritage, cultural diversity) and communication (press freedom, access to information). Its constitution emphasises building the 'defences of peace' in the minds of people. It has faced political controversies (US and UK withdrawals in the 1980s; US withdrawal over Palestine's admission in 2011 and later rejoining).

WHO (1948; Geneva): directs and coordinates international health; achievements include smallpox eradication (1980), polio campaigns, the Framework Convention on Tobacco Control, International Health Regulations, essential medicines, and responses to pandemics (COVID-19). Criticisms include delays and dependence on voluntary funding. Together, these specialised agencies show the functionalist idea that cooperation in technical and social fields can build peace and improve human welfare.
section-142: UNICEF (1946; New York): originally an emergency fund for children after the Second World War, now permanent; works on child survival, health, immunisation, nutrition, education, water and sanitation, protection from violence, exploitation and armed conflict, and emergency relief; advocates the Convention on the Rights of the Child; Nobel Peace Prize (1965). It is funded by voluntary contributions and has strong programmes in India.

UNDP (1965; New York): the UN's global development network, working in about 170 countries on poverty reduction, democratic governance, crisis prevention and recovery, climate change and sustainable development; coordinates the UN development system at country level; publishes the Human Development Report (since 1990) and the Human Development Index, which shifted the focus of development from income to human capabilities (Sen, Mahbub ul Haq). UNEP (1972; Nairobi): the leading environmental authority; facilitated agreements on the ozone layer (Montreal Protocol), biodiversity, hazardous waste and mercury; co-founded the IPCC; and promotes environmental awareness (World Environment Day).

Significance: these funds and programmes depend on voluntary contributions and work through partnerships with governments, NGOs and the private sector. They show that the UN's role extends beyond security to social welfare, development and the environment - areas directly affecting the lives of millions of people, including in India and Mizoram (for example, UNICEF's health and nutrition programmes).
section-143: New opportunities: with the end of Cold War rivalry, the Security Council could act more often - the Gulf War (1991), many new peacekeeping missions, sanctions regimes, international criminal tribunals (Yugoslavia 1993, Rwanda 1994) and post-conflict state-building (Cambodia, East Timor, Kosovo). The UN promoted democracy, human rights, development (MDGs 2000, SDGs 2015) and environmental protection (Rio Earth Summit 1992, Kyoto Protocol 1997, Paris Agreement 2015). Kofi Annan's leadership emphasised human rights and humanitarian intervention.

Problems and failures: failures in Somalia, Rwanda and Srebrenica; unilateral actions without UN approval (Kosovo 1999, Iraq 2003); the dominance of the USA in the unipolar moment; inadequate resources and peacekeeping scandals (cholera in Haiti, sexual abuse cases); financial crises; and new challenges - terrorism (the Counter-Terrorism Committee after 9/11), nuclear proliferation (North Korea, Iran), pandemics (COVID-19), climate change and refugee crises (over 100 million forcibly displaced people in 2023, according to UNHCR).

Recent trends: renewed great power rivalry (USA-China, Russia-West) has led to vetoes on Syria, Ukraine and Gaza, and a 'crisis of multilateralism'. Emerging powers such as India, Brazil and South Africa demand a greater role. Despite limitations, the UN remains the only universal forum for global cooperation, and its agencies provide essential services. The post-Cold War period thus showed both the potential and the limits of the UN.
section-144: Need for reform: the UN was designed for the world of 1945; membership has quadrupled; new powers have emerged (India, Brazil, Germany, Japan, African states); challenges have changed (terrorism, climate change, pandemics, cyber security); and the Security Council lacks representativeness and legitimacy, with the veto often blocking action. Management problems include bureaucracy, inefficiency, duplication and financial dependence.

Security Council reform: proposals for new permanent and non-permanent members (the G4 - India, Brazil, Germany, Japan; the African Union's Ezulwini Consensus; Uniting for Consensus); restricting the use of the veto (the French-Mexican initiative to refrain from veto in cases of mass atrocities, 2015; the General Assembly's 'veto initiative' of 2022 requiring the Assembly to debate whenever a veto is cast); improving working methods and transparency. India's case: the world's largest population and democracy, a major economy, nuclear power, large peacekeeping contributions, a founding member and a leader of developing countries. Obstacles: disagreement among regional rivals (Pakistan opposes India, Italy opposes Germany, China opposes Japan and is reluctant about India), and the need for P5 approval.

Other reforms: revitalising the General Assembly, strengthening ECOSOC and the Human Rights Council, management and budget reforms, a more transparent Secretary-General selection, strengthening peacekeeping and peacebuilding, and better coordination with regional organisations. The Pact for the Future (2024) reaffirmed commitments but concrete changes remain elusive. Reform is difficult because it requires agreement among states with different interests, especially the P5, but without reform, the UN's legitimacy and effectiveness may decline.
